title: Arkansas: Incorporation by Reference of Approved State Hazardous Waste Management Program
summary:
Here’s the short version: three federal updates touch food, waste oversight, and fisheries. The government set a residue limit for a fungicide on mangoes, formally recognized Arkansas’s hazardous waste rules under federal law, and temporarily increased this year’s Atlantic herring catch limit because a Canadian fishery landed less than expected.

For food and agriculture, the Environmental Protection Agency added a new tolerance for a fungicide on mangoes at one part per million. There are no approved uses of this product on U.S.-grown crops, so this mainly supports imported mangoes meeting a clear safety standard at the border. Importers, retailers, and consumers could see steadier supply. On the other hand, some consumers and advocacy groups may worry about any rise in allowable pesticide residues, even when set within safety margins, and organic producers may see little direct benefit.

On waste management, the Environmental Protection Agency updated the federal code to incorporate, by reference, Arkansas’s already approved hazardous waste program. This is a housekeeping move that makes it easier for the public and businesses to see which state rules are federally enforceable; it doesn’t add new requirements and takes effect December 18, 2025. State regulators and regulated facilities benefit from clearer alignment and easier compliance checks. Those who prefer direct federal control, or who rely on stricter state-only provisions, may note that “broader than federal” state rules aren’t enforceable by federal inspectors, which could create confusion about which rules apply in any given case.

In fisheries, federal managers increased the 2025 Atlantic herring catch limit by 1,000 metric tons for the rest of the year, and raised the allowance for the Gulf of Maine sub-area, after New Brunswick’s fishery in Canada caught less than a set threshold by October 1. This adjustment, effective through December 31, follows a preset formula and does not alter existing safeguards that slow catch when limits are nearly reached. Fishing vessels, processors, and coastal communities may gain short-term economic relief. Conservation groups and industries that depend on herring as forage—like tuna, whales, and seabirds—may worry about added pressure on a stressed stock, even if the increase is modest and temporary.

Taken together, these actions aim to clarify rules, smooth trade and supply, and implement a planned fisheries adjustment. The benefits are practical and near-term; the potential downsides center on longer-term health and ecosystem concerns that stakeholders will continue to watch.
